digests.standfirst: The attribution scientists who spent three weeks declining to say whether warming caused the Himalayan disaster published on 17 September and did something neither side of that argument expected: they refused the event-level question, attributed the conditions that produced it, and declared the event past the limits of what adaptation could have prevented. Within twenty-four hours Nepal's finance minister was in New Delhi using the finding. Meanwhile the Dutch budget answered a request to double water spending by funding the one thing the request said was already funded, and the United States finalised the repeal of its power-plant carbon rules on the floor of a G20 energy meeting whose only outcome document does not contain the word climate.

The UN's climate secretariat takes the security frame to the European Parliament and calls the summer a continent-wide economic security emergency; the Netherlands' delta commissioner asks the cabinet to double water spending to two per cent of GDP and says plainly that not all damage can now be prevented; and Nepal puts a $4.78 billion reconstruction bill to the world in the same week its scientists agree publicly that they cannot attribute the disaster that caused it.

The UN Environment Programme concedes that 1.5°C will be crossed and asks governments to manage the overshoot instead; small island states and Pacific leaders refuse the frame within forty-eight hours; and a Himalayan disaster turns into an argument about which monitoring system should have caught it.

Two multilateral instruments fail in one week, the military climate-security reporting infrastructure is found to have quietly stopped publishing, and attribution claims run wrong in both directions on two different disasters.
